intro.heading: The workshop went well. The law is still subtle.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care homes.
intro.paragraph: A trainer has spent an afternoon with the team on capacity, best interests and deprivation of liberty. People asked good questions and the feedback was positive. A few weeks later a carer tells a colleague that a resident with dementia "can't decide anything now", and another says a resident's choice to skip a meal should simply be overruled because it is unwise. Nobody did anything harmful, and nobody in the room spoke up. The manager realises the workshop covered the ideas, but she cannot say who left with them right. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A trainer runs the capacity and DoLS workshop for the team.
Good questions, lively discussion, warm feedback forms.
Everyone signs the attendance sheet and says it was useful.
A carer says a resident "can't decide anything" any more.
Another thinks an unwise choice means the person lacks capacity.
A new carer was too shy to say she had not followed the best interests part.
Signatures and warm feedback. Nothing that shows who understood.
“How do you decide whether a resident can make this choice?”

trail_close: The workshop was never the problem. The gap is between a good session and knowing what stuck. Here is how CareStream closes it, using your own policies, without replacing the session.

why.heading: Subtle ideas are the easiest to misunderstand
why.sub: People rarely say "I did not get that". They go back to the floor and act on what they think they heard.

cards.title: Nodding is not understanding
cards.body: Ideas such as capacity being decision specific or an unwise choice not meaning a lack of capacity sound obvious in the room. Under pressure, old habits come back.

cards.title: A small misreading has big effects
cards.body: Treating someone as unable to decide, or doing something to a person without asking, can affect their rights. Mistakes here are quiet, so nobody notices until later.

cards.title: Nobody checks what stuck
cards.body: A trainer cannot quiz every carer afterwards, and a manager cannot write extra lessons for every missed point. So the misunderstanding simply stays.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We ran a proper workshop. Why add anything on top?
items.a: You would not be replacing the workshop. You would be adding a check afterwards so you know what people took in. The room teaches and discusses. The follow up shows what stuck and gives a short lesson where it did not.

items.q: How do I check my carers understood capacity and best interests?
items.a: After the session you allocate the Mental Capacity Act and DoLS topic in the Training screen. The questions and lessons are built from your own policies where they cover it, and from general good practice where they do not. You can edit and preview them first. Carers answer in the Staff Hub on their own phone.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into that carer's Follow-up tab and they get an email, at most once a day and in English. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson (why this matters, what to remember, a realistic picture) then a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they like.

items.q: Our MCA and DoLS policy might be out of date. Does that matter?
items.a: Yes, and it is worth knowing. The lessons draw on your own wording, so an old policy teaches old wording. Where your policy does not cover a point, the lesson falls back on general good practice, which is a prompt to review it. Check your policy against current guidance and with your local authority, and update it before you allocate.

items.q: Will it tell me what the law says now about the Liberty Protection Safeguards?
items.a: No. CareStream does not decide which legal scheme applies, and this page does not either. Keep your policy in line with current official guidance and your local authority, and let your policy be the source for the training.

items.q: Do I get an alert every time someone answers wrongly?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the pattern in Analytics under Knowledge gaps, which shows open gaps, staff affected and the most missed questions, and a digest arrives on Monday.

items.q: Can staff do this in another language?
items.a: Yes, on the paid plans. A carer whose second language is easier for legal ideas can open the lesson in it, so a wrong answer points to a gap in knowledge and not in vocabulary. Reminder emails stay in English.

items.q: How do I try it, and what does it show an inspector?
items.a: Create a free account and start the 14 day free trial, then allocate one module after your next session. You can show what each person was asked, what they got wrong, the lesson they were given and whether it then landed. It sits alongside the rest of your CQC evidence.

limits.heading: A check on understanding, not a legal adviser

cards.title: It does not make capacity decisions
cards.body: Whether a person has capacity for a particular decision, and what is in their best interests, are assessments made by people. CareStream checks that staff understand the ideas.

cards.title: It does not tell you which scheme applies
cards.body: It cannot judge whether a restriction needs an application, or which legal scheme applies. For that, follow current guidance and speak to your local authority.

cards.title: It does not alert you to every wrong answer
cards.body: The picture reaches you through the Knowledge gaps view and the Monday digest. Ad hoc training and translation are on the paid plans.

faqs.heading: Mental capacity training and CareStream, answered

items.q: What should mental capacity act training cover for care staff?
items.a: At the least, the five principles in section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005: assume capacity, help people decide, an unwise choice is not a lack of capacity, act in best interests, and choose the less restrictive option. Add how your own home records decisions.

items.q: Where can I find the official guidance on the Act?
items.a: The Mental Capacity Act Code of Practice on gov.uk explains what you must do when you act or make decisions on behalf of people who cannot. Your policy should be consistent with it.

items.q: Is a mental capacity act quiz enough on its own?
items.a: A mental capacity act quiz shows what people can recall, which is a start. Real practice needs conversations, supervision and observation. Use the quiz as a check for understanding and a way to find who needs a conversation.

items.q: What is the difference between MCA and DoLS training?
items.a: The Act covers capacity and best interests. DoLS training is about deprivation of liberty and when to raise it. Many homes run MCA and DoLS training as one session, so check understanding of both.

items.q: Does a knowledge check replace the workshop?
items.a: No. A knowledge check after the workshop shows what stuck. For hands on practice and discussion, you still need a competent person in the room.

items.q: What if a carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It appears in their Follow-up tab. They can choose Learn & retry, a short lesson on that point followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question, as often as they need. Treat it as information, not failure.

items.q: Where do I check the current position on DoLS and the Liberty Protection Safeguards?
items.a: Check current official guidance and ask your local authority, as the position has changed over time and we do not state it here. Then make sure your policy and your MCA and DoLS course match it.

items.q: Do we need deprivation of liberty safeguards training every year?
items.a: How often you refresh deprivation of liberty safeguards training is a decision for your policy and your training plan. Many homes include it in an annual training plan and add an ad hoc check when practice slips.

items.q: Does CareStream write our MCA policy?
items.a: No. It builds lessons from the policies you already have and shows where they are silent. See policy gap detection for how it highlights missing cover.

guide.heading: How to follow up an MCA and DoLS workshop
guide.lede: A short, practical routine you can run after any session on capacity and deprivation of liberty. It takes a few minutes of your time.

paragraphs: Read your own policy first. If it is old, update it before you teach from it, because staff will follow what is written down. Then decide which three or four ideas matter most for your residents, such as how you support a person to decide and how you record it.
Within a few days, allocate a short module on the topic to everyone who attended. Keep it to a handful of questions so it fits into a shift.
checklist: Update your MCA and DoLS policy against current guidance and your local authority
Allocate the topic module and preview the questions first
Give staff a due date a few days after the session
Open Knowledge gaps after a week and talk to anyone who is stuck

sections.h3: What to do with the results
paragraphs: If one question is missed by many people, the session needs a second go. If one person misses several, have a quiet conversation. For understanding to turn into practice, watch it in the care you see every day, as in the picture of a carer offering a choice and a manager observing.

guide.note: This guide is practical advice, not legal advice. Follow current official guidance and speak to your local authority on legal questions.
